routes.description: Establish that contingent existence, religious experience, or moral obligation provides a defensible inference to an objective transcendent ground identifiable with God.
routes.successCriteria: At least one affirmative line must connect the relevant experience or fact to a necessary, objective, and non-arbitrary divine ground while answering the principal non-theistic alternative.

motionBridge.description: Show that at least one of the three proposed domains warrants affirming God's existence rather than merely describing human thought or feeling.

centralBridges.description: Connect experienced contingent beings and their totality to an external sufficient reason that does not itself require a further explanation.
Show that the character of religious experience is better explained by an objective transcendent cause than by a wholly subjective account.
Connect objective moral obligation and the authority of moral law to a transcendent ground of value that is neither arbitrary nor socially contingent.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Distinguish an experiential inference to a necessary being from an a priori attempt to define that being into existence.
Explain how moral disagreement and culturally variable precepts remain open to criticism by reference to an objective ideal order.

routes.description: Show that the contingency, religious-experience, and moral-obligation arguments do not require God because their key inferences are invalid, underdetermined, or matched by non-theistic explanations.
routes.successCriteria: Prevent each affirmative line from reaching its divine conclusion by challenging its central inference or supplying an adequate account that does not presuppose a transcendent being.

motionBridge.description: Show that none of the proposed domains supplies sufficient grounds for moving from observed experience or practice to God's existence.

centralBridges.description: Challenge the application of necessity to beings and the inference from explanations of particular contingent things to an explanation of their totality.
Show that private experiences and their beneficial effects cannot discriminate an external divine object from subjective or incompatible interpretations.
Account for moral discrimination and obligation through feeling, custom, education, or imagined social disapproval without invoking divine authority.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Require that claims about a being whose essence includes existence avoid treating existence as a predicate or reviving an ontological inference.
Use historical and cultural variation in perceived duties to test the asserted universality and absoluteness of moral law.

sections.title: Contingency and the meaning of necessary existence
sections.rationale: This issue governs whether an empirically encountered contingent being can support a coherent modal inference to a being that cannot fail to exist.

sections.title: The totality of contingent beings and sufficient reason
sections.rationale: This issue tests the indispensable move from explanations within the world to an external explanation of the world or totality as such.

sections.title: Religious experience and an objective transcendent cause
sections.rationale: This issue addresses whether the distinctive character of mystical awareness supplies grounds for an objective divine reality rather than a subjective event.

sections.title: Competing reports and transformative effects
sections.rationale: This issue determines whether conviction, beneficial transformation, and experiential veracity can distinguish divine contact from incompatible or fictional objects.

sections.title: Moral feeling, objective value, and critical standards
sections.rationale: This issue concerns whether moral distinctions require an objective standard and whether identifying goodness with a divine source establishes rather than assumes God.

sections.title: Moral obligation, variation, and its explanatory ground
sections.rationale: This issue tests whether the authoritative sense of obligation requires a transcendent lawgiver or is adequately explained by historical customs, education, and social disapproval.
